title: Asthma in adults: diagnosis and AIR/MART treatment
blurb: Apply the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guideline: objective diagnosis, ICS/formoterol AIR and MART, technique, adherence and action plans.
question: Ms Rossi, 29, has confirmed asthma and uses only a salbutamol inhaler, which she needs most days. Under the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline (NG245), what should her treatment be changed to?

teach.h: A new model of asthma care
teach.body: Formally: NG245 (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024) covers diagnosis, monitoring and chronic management of asthma; it replaced NICE NG80 and parts of SIGN 158, but does not cover acute attacks. In plain English: asthma is now diagnosed with objective tests rather than symptoms alone, and adults (12 and over) are treated with one inhaler containing both an inhaled steroid and formoterol, used as the reliever, instead of salbutamol alone.
teach.cite: NICE NG245 (2024); acute attacks remain in SIGN 158

steps.label: Eosinophils or FeNO
steps.sub: eosinophils above range or FeNO 50 ppb+

steps.label: Reversibility
steps.sub: FEV1 up 12% or more and 200 mL or more

steps.label: PEF variability
steps.sub: twice daily for 2 weeks, 20% or more

teach.caption: Move to the next test if the previous one does not confirm asthma. Do not confirm a diagnosis without a suggestive history and a supporting objective test; code as 'suspected asthma' until then (1.1.2).
NG245 1.7.1–1.7.4. As of November 2025 only certain budesonide/formoterol inhalers were licensed for AIR; others would be off-label.

levels.label: Moderate-dose MART + LTRA or LAMA trial

teach.caption: Highly symptomatic at diagnosis (e.g. regular night waking) or a severe exacerbation: start at low-dose MART (1.7.2). If moderate-dose MART fails, check FeNO and eosinophils: raised = refer (1.7.5).

teach.h: Before stepping up, check the basics
teach.body: Uncontrolled asthma is often not a drug problem. NG245 1.6.1 asks you first to consider alternative diagnoses, adherence (check prescription records), inhaler technique, smoking or vaping, occupational exposures and other triggers. Observe the person using their inhaler (and spacer) at every review and whenever control worsens or the device changes. Review the response 8 to 12 weeks after any change.

rows.label: Reliever use, checked on prescription record

teach.note: Do not use regular PEF monitoring to assess control unless it is part of the personalised action plan. Consider FeNO at review and before and after changing treatment.

items: Offer a self-management programme: a documented personalised action plan plus education.
In adults the plan may be based on symptoms, peak flow or both.
Review the plan, and check it is understood, at hospital admission, acute consultations and annual reviews.
Adults on a single ICS inhaler (not MART): the plan can include an increased ICS dose for 7 days when control deteriorates.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Ms Rossi at an asthma review
teach.body: Ms Rossi uses salbutamol alone most days. Asthma nurse Grace explains that NG245 advises against SABA without an inhaled steroid (1.6.3) and that people using a SABA alone should change to as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR, 1.7.7). Grace watches her use the new dry powder inhaler, corrects her technique, writes a personalised action plan with her and books a review in 8 to 12 weeks.

teach.text: Do not confuse the guidelines: NG245 (2024) covers diagnosis and long-term care, and SALBUTAMOL-ONLY treatment is now outdated. Acute attacks are still managed with SIGN 158 (salbutamol nebulisers, steroids, oxygen 94–98%). And FeNO cut-off for adults is 50 ppb, not the 35 ppb used for children.

items: Diagnose with history plus an objective test: eosinophils/FeNO, then reversibility, then PEF, then challenge.
New diagnosis (12+): as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR); then low-dose MART, then moderate-dose MART.
Never leave someone on SABA alone: switch SABA-only users to AIR.
Check adherence, technique, smoking and triggers before stepping up; review in 8–12 weeks.
Everyone gets a personalised action plan, reviewed at admissions and annual reviews.

summary: You can now describe how asthma is objectively diagnosed in adults under NG245 and how AIR and MART regimens are used and stepped up. You can also check control, adherence and inhaler technique, and support a personalised action plan.

A.q: Which result supports a diagnosis of asthma in an adult with a suggestive history under NG245?
options: FeNO of 50 ppb or more
FeNO of 25 ppb or more
FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7
FeNO of 35 ppb or more
A.why: NG245 1.2.1: diagnose asthma in adults if the eosinophil count is above the reference range or FeNO is 50 ppb or more.

whyNot.1: 25 ppb is below the adult diagnostic level.
whyNot.2: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 defines airflow obstruction in COPD, not an asthma diagnostic test.
whyNot.3: 35 ppb is the threshold for children aged 5 to 16.

A.q: What is the recommended initial treatment for a 34-year-old with newly diagnosed asthma who is not highly symptomatic?
options: Salbutamol as needed
Regular low-dose ICS plus salbutamol
Low-dose ICS/formoterol as needed
Montelukast once daily
A.why: NG245 1.7.1: offer a low-dose ICS/formoterol combination inhaler taken as needed (AIR therapy) to people aged 12 and over with newly diagnosed asthma.

whyNot.0: SABA without an ICS should not be prescribed (1.6.3).
whyNot.1: Regular ICS plus SABA is the older model; AIR is now first-line.
whyNot.3: An LTRA is a later add-on trial, not initial treatment.

A.q: After a change in asthma medicines, when does NG245 advise reviewing the response?
options: After 2 to 4 weeks
At the annual review
After 6 months
After 8 to 12 weeks
A.why: NG245 1.6.4: review the response to treatment 8 to 12 weeks after starting or adjusting medicines.

whyNot.0: 2 to 4 weeks is shorter than the NG245 interval.
whyNot.1: Waiting for the annual review is too long after a change.
whyNot.2: 6 months is too long to wait after a change.

B.q: A man's asthma is not controlled on as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol. His technique and adherence are good. What is the next step?
options: Add a regular SABA
Add oral prednisolone daily
Refer for bronchial challenge
Start low-dose MART
B.why: NG245 1.7.3: offer low-dose MART to people aged 12 and over whose asthma is not controlled on as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol.

whyNot.0: Adding regular SABA is not part of the NG245 pathway.
whyNot.1: Maintenance oral steroids are not the next step.
whyNot.2: Bronchial challenge is a diagnostic test, not a treatment step.

B.q: An adult's asthma remains uncontrolled. Which question should the nurse explore first, before any treatment change?
options: How she uses her inhaler, and how often
Whether she has tried a nebuliser
Whether a stronger steroid is available
Whether she can have oral steroids
B.why: NG245 1.6.1: address possible reasons for uncontrolled asthma, including adherence and inhaler technique, before starting or adjusting medicines.

whyNot.1: Nebulisers are not part of long-term asthma management.
whyNot.2: Escalating ICS before checking adherence and technique is premature.
whyNot.3: Oral steroids treat attacks, not uncontrolled chronic asthma.

B.q: Which statement about peak flow monitoring in adult asthma is correct under NG245?
options: Regular PEF should be used to judge control
PEF is used if it is in the action plan
PEF replaces symptom questions at review
PEF must be recorded twice daily for life
B.why: NG245 1.5.3: do not use regular PEF monitoring to assess control unless there are person-specific reasons, such as when PEF is part of the personalised action plan.

whyNot.0: NG245 advises against routine regular PEF monitoring for control.
whyNot.2: Symptoms, reliever use, steroid courses and admissions are reviewed at every visit.
whyNot.3: Twice-daily PEF for 2 weeks is a diagnostic test, not lifelong monitoring.

C.q: Mr Hughes, 45, has suspected asthma. His FeNO is 30 ppb and eosinophils are normal. Spirometry is delayed by 6 weeks. What does NG245 advise next?
options: Confirm asthma on symptoms and start AIR
Measure PEF twice daily for 2 weeks
Refer straight for bronchial challenge
Repeat FeNO after 6 weeks of ICS
C.why: NG245 1.2.3: if spirometry is not available or delayed, measure PEF twice daily for 2 weeks; diagnose asthma if variability is 20% or more.

whyNot.0: A diagnosis needs a supporting objective test; code as suspected until then.
whyNot.2: Challenge testing comes after eosinophils, FeNO, reversibility and PEF have not confirmed it.
whyNot.3: ICS makes FeNO more likely to be normal, so it would not help diagnosis.

C.q: Mrs Baptiste, 52, is on moderate-dose MART with good adherence and technique but remains uncontrolled. Her FeNO is raised. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Refer to a specialist in asthma care
Add an LTRA for an 8 to 12 week trial
Switch back to as-needed AIR therapy
Add a separate salbutamol inhaler
C.why: NG245 1.7.5: if not controlled on moderate-dose MART despite good adherence, check FeNO and eosinophils; if either is raised, refer to a specialist in asthma care.

whyNot.1: An LTRA or LAMA trial is considered when neither FeNO nor eosinophils is raised.
whyNot.3: MART already provides the reliever, and SABA adds no anti-inflammatory cover.

C.q: A woman with asthma is admitted after an attack and is now recovering on the ward. What should the nurse do with her personalised asthma action plan?
options: Leave it for her GP to update later
Review it and check she understands it
Replace it with a peak flow diary
Remove it as admission shows it failed
C.why: NG245 1.14.2: review the content of the personalised action plan and check the person understands it at hospital admission, acute consultations and annual reviews.

whyNot.0: Hospital admission is a point where the plan should be reviewed, not deferred.
whyNot.2: A diary does not replace a personalised action plan.
whyNot.3: The plan is reviewed and improved, not removed.

reteach.title: One inhaler does two jobs
reteach.question: Why does a single ICS/formoterol inhaler work as both reliever and preventer?

blocks.h: Fast relief with steroid on board
blocks.body: Formoterol opens the airways within minutes, so it relieves symptoms like salbutamol. Because the same puff contains an inhaled steroid, every time the person reaches for relief they also treat the inflammation. With AIR they use it only when needed. With MART they also take regular maintenance doses. Salbutamol alone relieves symptoms but leaves the inflammation untreated, which is why NG245 moves SABA-only users to AIR.

blocks.text: AIR and MART are for people aged 12 and over. Children under 12 follow a separate paediatric pathway in NG245.

explain.body: History plus a test. Adults: eosinophils above range or FeNO 50 ppb or more; then reversibility (FEV1 up 12% and 200 mL); then PEF variability 20% over 2 weeks; then bronchial challenge.

test.q: What FEV1 change after a bronchodilator supports asthma in an adult under NG245?
options: Rise of 12% or more and 200 mL or more
Rise of 5% or more and 100 mL or more
Rise of 20% or more in peak flow
Rise of 400 mL with an FEV1/FVC of 0.6
test.why: NG245 1.2.2: diagnose asthma if FEV1 increases by 12% or more and 200 mL or more (or by 10% or more of predicted normal FEV1).

whyNot.1: 5% and 100 mL is below the NG245 threshold.
whyNot.2: 20% PEF variability is measured over 2 weeks, not as reversibility.
whyNot.3: This mixes a COPD obstruction ratio with an older reversibility figure.

explain.body: New asthma: as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol (AIR). Not controlled: low-dose MART, then moderate-dose MART. Highly symptomatic at diagnosis: start with low-dose MART.

test.q: A newly diagnosed adult wakes with asthma most nights. Which treatment should she start on?
options: As-needed AIR therapy
Low-dose MART
Salbutamol as needed
Regular high-dose ICS
test.why: NG245 1.7.2: if highly symptomatic (for example regular nocturnal waking) or presenting with a severe exacerbation, start with low-dose MART.

whyNot.0: AIR is for newly diagnosed asthma without these features.
whyNot.2: SABA without ICS is not recommended.
whyNot.3: High-dose ICS is not a starting treatment.

explain.body: Observe inhaler use at every review, when control worsens and when the device changes. Check adherence with prescription records. A spacer is usually prescribed with a metered dose inhaler.

test.q: When does NG245 say the person's inhaler technique should be observed?
options: At diagnosis and then every 5 years
When the person asks for help
At every asthma review
When a new prescriber takes over
test.why: NG245 1.6.7: observe the person using their inhaler at every asthma review (routine or unscheduled), every asthma-related consultation, when control worsens, when the device changes, or when asked.

whyNot.0: Five-yearly checks are far too infrequent.
whyNot.1: Asking is one trigger, but checks happen at every review.
whyNot.3: A change of prescriber is not the trigger listed.

explain.body: Every adult with asthma is offered a documented personalised action plan plus education, based on symptoms, PEF or both. It is reviewed at admissions, acute consultations and annual reviews.

test.q: What does an asthma self-management programme consist of under NG245?
options: A peak flow meter and a symptom diary
A rescue pack of oral antibiotics
An action plan plus education
A home nebuliser and a leaflet
test.why: NG245 1.14.1: offer an asthma self-management programme comprising a documented personalised action plan and education.

whyNot.0: A meter and diary alone are not the programme described.
whyNot.1: Antibiotic rescue packs belong to COPD action plans.
whyNot.3: Nebulisers are not part of chronic asthma self-management.
